title: Migrating a PostgreSQL Database to Managed Cloud with Less Than 5 Minutes of Downtime
summary:
Moving a production PostgreSQL instance from a self-hosted StatefulSet (or a bare-metal VM) to RDS, Cloud SQL or Azure Database is one of those migrations everyone postpones, because the default plan is "pg_dump on Saturday at 2 a.m. and pray". For a 400 GB database that plan means a four-hour outage, a tired on-call engineer, and no realistic rollback.

There is a better option that has been available since PostgreSQL 10: logical replication. You keep the old database serving traffic while the new managed instance catches up in the background, then you flip the connection string during a short, controlled freeze. This article is the concrete runbook: prerequisites, bootstrap, lag control, the cutover itself, and the rollback path.

Context: why the dump-and-restore window kills you

A pg_dump/pg_restore migration has a downtime cost that scales linearly with data volume and index count. Roughly:

  • dump: 10–20 minutes per 100 GB with -Fd -j 4
  • transfer to the cloud: bounded by your egress bandwidth
  • restore: index rebuild dominates, often 2–3× the dump time
  • post-restore ANALYZE: another 5–20 minutes before the planner behaves

You cannot accept writes during any of that. And if something goes wrong at minute 180, your rollback is "restart the old database" — which is fine, except you just burned the whole maintenance window.

Logical replication inverts the cost model. The expensive part (initial copy + catch-up) happens while the source is live. The only thing left in the maintenance window is: stop writes, wait for the last WAL bytes to be applied, fix sequences, switch the app. That is a 2–5 minute operation, doable at 11 a.m. on a Tuesday.

The budget we are targeting:

Step Target
Freeze writes (scale down / PgBouncer PAUSE) 20 s
Drain replication lag to 0 30–60 s
Sync sequences 10 s
Switch DSN + rollout 60–120 s
Smoke tests 60 s

Step 0: pre-flight checks

Source prerequisites

Logical replication requires wal_level = logical on the source. On a self-managed instance this is a restart-only parameter — plan it a few days ahead, it is the only mandatory restart of the whole migration.

# On the source (psql as superuser)
psql -c "SHOW wal_level;"          # must be 'logical'
psql -c "SHOW max_replication_slots;"   # >= existing slots + 1
psql -c "SHOW max_wal_senders;"         # >= existing senders + 1
psql -c "SHOW max_slot_wal_keep_size;"  # PG13+: cap WAL retention, e.g. '50GB'

For a StatefulSet-managed Postgres, patch the config and do a rolling restart:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: postgres-tuning
  namespace: data
data:
  99-logical.conf: |
    wal_level = logical
    max_replication_slots = 10
    max_wal_senders = 10
    max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB

Then validate that every table you intend to replicate has a primary key. Logical replication applies UPDATE/DELETE by replica identity; a table without a PK silently breaks the subscription.

SELECT c.relname
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind = 'r'
  AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')
  AND c.relreplident = 'd'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = c.oid AND i.indisprimary);

Fix each hit with a PK, or ALTER TABLE x REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; (acceptable only for small, low-churn tables — it is expensive).

Target prerequisites

  • RDS: set rds.logical_replication = 1 in the parameter group (static, requires reboot) and grant rds_replication to the migration role. For RDS acting as subscriber you need rds_superuser.
  • Cloud SQL: enable the cloudsql.logical_decoding flag and cloudsql.enable_pglogical if you use pglogical; the migration user needs the REPLICATION attribute (cloudsqlsuperuser).
  • Match major versions, or go source ≤ target. Logical replication tolerates a newer subscriber; the reverse is unsupported.

Network path

This trips up most teams: the subscriber connects to the publisher, not the other way around. Your RDS instance must be able to open a TCP session to your source Postgres. In practice that means a VPN/Direct Connect, a public endpoint restricted by security group, or an SSH/stunnel bastion. Validate it before writing a single line of SQL.

# From a pod in the target VPC
oc run netcheck --rm -it --image=registry.redhat.io/rhel9/support-tools -- \
  bash -c 'timeout 5 bash -c "

Step 1: bootstrap the schema

Native logical replication copies data only. Schema, indexes, sequences, extensions and grants are your job. Dump with a client matching the target major version.

PGSSLMODE=require pg_dump \
  --schema-only --no-owner --no-privileges \
  --exclude-schema='pg_*' \
  -h pg-source.internal -U migrator -d appdb \
  -f schema.sql

# Review it: strip anything the managed service rejects
grep -nE 'CREATE EXTENSION|ALTER .* OWNER|tablespace' schema.sql

psql "host=appdb.abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com user=migrator dbname=appdb sslmode=verify-full" \
  -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f schema.sql

Run it as a Job so it is reproducible and auditable:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: pg-schema-bootstrap
  namespace: data
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: psql
          image: quay.io/enterprisedb/postgresql:16
          command: ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
          args:
            - |
              set -euo pipefail
              pg_dump --schema-only --no-owner --no-privileges \
                -d "$SOURCE_URL" -f /tmp/schema.sql
              psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d "$TARGET_URL" -f /tmp/schema.sql
          env:
            - name: SOURCE_URL
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: pg-migration, key: source-url } }
            - name: TARGET_URL
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: pg-migration, key: target-url } }
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            runAsNonRoot: true
            capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
            seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }

Performance tip: for databases above ~200 GB, restore the schema without secondary indexes (pg_dump --schema-only then filter CREATE INDEX), let the initial copy run, and create the indexes afterwards with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Initial copy into an index-free table is 3–5× faster.

Step 2: start replication

Native logical replication (PostgreSQL 10+)

On the source:

CREATE PUBLICATION mig_pub FOR ALL TABLES;
-- or, scoped: CREATE PUBLICATION mig_pub FOR TABLE public.orders, public.customers;

On the target (RDS/Cloud SQL):

CREATE SUBSCRIPTION mig_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=pg-source.internal port=5432 dbname=appdb user=repl password=... sslmode=verify-full'
  PUBLICATION mig_pub
  WITH (copy_data = true, create_slot = true, slot_name = 'mig_slot', streaming = on);

This creates a replication slot on the source named mig_slot. From that instant, the source retains WAL for the subscriber. That is exactly what guarantees zero data loss — and exactly what fills your source disk if the subscription stalls. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size and alert on retained bytes (next section).

Initial copy progress is visible on the subscriber:

SELECT srsubid, srrelid::regclass AS table, srsubstate  -- i=init, d=copying, f=finished, r=ready
FROM pg_subscription_rel ORDER BY srsubstate;

When to use pglogical instead

pglogical is worth the extra extension when:

  • the source runs PostgreSQL 9.4–9.6 (native logical replication does not exist there);
  • you need sequence replication (pglogical.create_replication_set(..., ) plus pglogical.synchronize_sequence()), which native logical replication does not provide;
  • you want row/column filtering and conflict resolution policies on PG < 15.

Both RDS and Cloud SQL ship pglogical. Setup is symmetric: pglogical.create_node() on both sides, pglogical.create_subscription() on the target.

When to use DMS

AWS DMS is the right tool for heterogeneous migrations (Oracle → Postgres) or when the source version is too old for logical decoding. For Postgres → Postgres, DMS CDC adds a moving part, remaps types imperfectly, and still does not handle sequences or DDL. Prefer native replication; keep DMS as the fallback.

Step 3: treat replication lag as an SLO

You cannot cut over blind. Two queries matter.

On the source, how far behind is the subscriber:

SELECT application_name, state,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), sent_lsn))   AS send_lag,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)) AS total_lag,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication
WHERE application_name = 'mig_sub';

SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained_wal
FROM pg_replication_slots;

On the target:

SELECT subname, latest_end_lsn, latest_end_time, now() - latest_end_time AS staleness
FROM pg_stat_subscription;

Wire this into Prometheus with postgres_exporter and a custom query, then alert:

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: pg-migration-lag
  namespace: data
  labels:
    role: alert-rules
spec:
  groups:
    - name: pg-migration
      rules:
        - alert: PgLogicalReplicationLagHigh
          expr: pg_replication_lag_bytes{application_name="mig_sub"} > 5.24288e+08
          for: 5m
          labels: { severity: warning }
          annotations:
            summary: "Subscriber mig_sub is more than 500 MB behind"
        - alert: PgReplicationSlotRetainingWal
          expr: pg_replication_slot_retained_bytes{slot_name="mig_slot"} > 2.0e+10
          for: 10m
          labels: { severity: critical }
          annotations:
            summary: "mig_slot retains >20 GB of WAL — source disk at risk"
        - alert: PgSubscriptionInactive
          expr: pg_replication_slot_active{slot_name="mig_slot"} == 0
          for: 2m
          labels: { severity: critical }

Let the subscription run for at least 24 hours before cutover. You want to see it survive your nightly batch, your VACUUM window, and a deploy.

Step 4: the cutover runbook

1. Freeze writes

The cleanest freeze in Kubernetes/OpenShift is to scale the writers to zero and park the connection pooler:

# Record current replicas for rollback
oc get deploy -n app -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}={.spec.replicas}{"\n"}{end}' > replicas.txt

oc scale deploy/api deploy/worker deploy/scheduler -n app --replicas=0
oc wait --for=delete pod -l 'app in (api,worker,scheduler)' -n app --timeout=90s

Belt and braces on the source — block anything that slipped through:

ALTER DATABASE appdb SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'appdb' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() AND usename <> 'repl';

2. Drain the lag to zero 

psql -d "$SOURCE_URL" -At -c "
  SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)
  FROM pg_stat_replication WHERE application_name='mig_sub';"

Loop until it returns 0. With writes stopped this takes seconds.

3. Synchronise sequences

This is the step people forget, and it produces duplicate-key errors ten minutes after go-live. Generate the setval statements on the source and replay them on the target:

psql -d "$SOURCE_URL" -At -c "
  SELECT format('SELECT setval(%L, %s, true);',
                schemaname||'.'||sequencename,
                COALESCE(last_value, 1))
  FROM pg_sequences
  WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema');" \
| psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d "$TARGET_URL"

4. Switch the application

Keep the DSN in a Secret so the switch is one oc patch + rollout, not a code change.

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: app-db
  namespace: app
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secretsmanager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: app-db
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: DATABASE_URL
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/appdb/dsn        # value updated to the RDS endpoint at cutover

# Flip the pointer, then bring the app back
oc annotate externalsecret/app-db -n app force-sync="$(date +%s)" --overwrite
oc scale deploy/api -n app --replicas=6
oc rollout status deploy/api -n app --timeout=180s

5. Verify, then detach 

# Row-count parity on the top tables
for t in orders customers invoices; do
  s=$(psql -At -d "$SOURCE_URL" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM $t")
  d=$(psql -At -d "$TARGET_URL" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM $t")
  printf "%-12s source=%-10s target=%-10s %s\n" "$t" "$s" "$d" \
    "$([ "$s" = "$d" ] && echo OK || echo MISMATCH)"
done

psql -d "$TARGET_URL" -c "ANALYZE;"

Only after the application is healthy:

-- On the target
ALTER SUBSCRIPTION mig_sub DISABLE;
-- Later, once rollback is no longer an option:
DROP SUBSCRIPTION mig_sub;   -- also drops the slot on the source

Do not drop the subscription immediately — DROP SUBSCRIPTION removes the replication slot, and with it your cheap rollback.

Step 5: rollback

Two tiers, pick based on risk appetite.

Tier 1 — within the first minutes. The source is still intact and read-only. Revert the DSN, re-enable writes, scale back up:

psql -d "$SOURCE_URL" -c "ALTER DATABASE appdb SET default_transaction_read_only = off;"
# restore previous DSN in the secret store, then
oc annotate externalsecret/app-db -n app force-sync="$(date +%s)" --overwrite
oc rollout restart deploy/api -n app

Cost: you lose any writes already committed to the target. Acceptable only in the first minutes, which is why smoke tests must be fast and automated.

Tier 2 — reverse replication. Before re-opening writes, create a publication on the target and a subscription on the source with copy_data = false. Writes then flow back, and rollback becomes lossless for hours. This doubles the setup work and requires the reverse network path, but for a payments or ordering database it is worth it.

-- On the target (new primary)
CREATE PUBLICATION back_pub FOR ALL TABLES;
-- On the old source
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION back_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=appdb.abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com dbname=appdb user=repl sslmode=verify-full'
  PUBLICATION back_pub WITH (copy_data = false, slot_name = 'back_slot');

Remember to re-run the sequence sync in the reverse direction if you ever use it.

Security best practices

Dedicated replication role, least privilege. Do not reuse the application user. The source role needs only REPLICATION plus SELECT on replicated tables:

CREATE ROLE repl WITH LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD :'pw';
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE appdb TO repl;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO repl;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO repl;

Force TLS end to end. Logical replication streams plaintext row data. Use sslmode=verify-full with an explicit sslrootcert, never require (which does not verify the hostname). Set rds.force_ssl=1 / cloudsql requireSsl on the target, and hostssl only in the source pg_hba.conf:

hostssl appdb repl 10.42.0.0/16 scram-sha-256

Never put the DSN in a manifest. Use External Secrets, Vault, or at minimum a sealed secret. The CREATE SUBSCRIPTION connection string containing the password is stored in pg_subscription and visible to superusers — rotate that password right after cutover.

Restrict the network path. The source must only be reachable from the target's NAT egress IPs, and the migration Jobs must only reach the two databases:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-migration-egress
  namespace: data
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { job-name: pg-schema-bootstrap }
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.42.10.0/24 }   # source Postgres
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.43.20.0/24 }   # RDS subnet
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: openshift-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }

Harden the pods. The Job above runs runAsNonRoot, drops all capabilities and uses RuntimeDefault seccomp, so it passes the restricted-v2 SCC without exceptions. Never run migration tooling as a cluster-admin service account.

Keep an audit trail. Enable log_replication_commands = on on the source during the migration window, and snapshot the source (EBS snapshot / volume snapshot) immediately before the freeze. Replication is not a backup.

Key takeaways

  • Logical replication moves the expensive work out of the maintenance window. The only serialised steps are freeze, drain, sequences, switch — 2 to 5 minutes regardless of database size.
  • wal_level = logical is your only mandatory restart. Schedule it days ahead and the cutover itself needs no restart at all.
  • Replication slots are a loaded gun. They guarantee durability and they fill your source disk. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size, alert on retained WAL, and never leave an inactive slot behind.
  • Sequences and indexes are not replicated. Script the setval sync, and build secondary indexes after the initial copy with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
  • Monitor with pg_stat_replication and pg_stat_subscription, not with hope. Cut over only when the byte lag is literally zero.
  • Keep the subscription disabled, not dropped, for 24–48 hours. Dropping it destroys the slot and your fast rollback. For high-stakes data, invest in reverse replication before re-opening writes.
  • pglogical for old sources and sequence replication, DMS for heterogeneous migrations, native logical replication for everything else.

Rehearse the whole runbook against a restored snapshot first. The second time you execute it, five minutes will feel generous.

        - alert: PgReplicationSlotRetainingWal
          expr: pg_replication_slot_retained_bytes{slot_name="mig_slot"} > 2.0e+10
          for: 10m
          labels: { severity: critical }
          annotations:
            summary: "mig_slot retains >20 GB of WAL — source disk at risk"
        - alert: PgSubscriptionInactive
          expr: pg_replication_slot_active{slot_name="mig_slot"} == 0
          for: 2m
          labels: { severity: critical }

Let the subscription run for at least 24 hours before cutover. You want to see it survive your nightly batch, your VACUUM window, and a deploy.

Step 4: the cutover runbook

1. Freeze writes

The cleanest freeze in Kubernetes/OpenShift is to scale the writers to zero and park the connection pooler:

# Record current replicas for rollback
oc get deploy -n app -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}={.spec.replicas}{"\n"}{end}' > replicas.txt

oc scale deploy/api deploy/worker deploy/scheduler -n app --replicas=0
oc wait --for=delete pod -l 'app in (api,worker,scheduler)' -n app --timeout=90s

Belt and braces on the source — block anything that slipped through:

ALTER DATABASE appdb SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'appdb' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() AND usename <> 'repl';

2. Drain the lag to zero 

psql -d "$SOURCE_URL" -At -c "
  SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)
  FROM pg_stat_replication WHERE application_name='mig_sub';"

Loop until it returns 0. With writes stopped this takes seconds.

3. Synchronise sequences

This is the step people forget, and it produces duplicate-key errors ten minutes after go-live. Generate the setval statements on the source and replay them on the target:

psql -d "$SOURCE_URL" -At -c "
  SELECT format('SELECT setval(%L, %s, true);',
                schemaname||'.'||sequencename,
                COALESCE(last_value, 1))
  FROM pg_sequences
  WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema');" \
| psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d "$TARGET_URL"

4. Switch the application

Keep the DSN in a Secret so the switch is one oc patch + rollout, not a code change.

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: app-db
  namespace: app
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secretsmanager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: app-db
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: DATABASE_URL
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/appdb/dsn        # value updated to the RDS endpoint at cutover

# Flip the pointer, then bring the app back
oc annotate externalsecret/app-db -n app force-sync="$(date +%s)" --overwrite
oc scale deploy/api -n app --replicas=6
oc rollout status deploy/api -n app --timeout=180s

5. Verify, then detach 

# Row-count parity on the top tables
for t in orders customers invoices; do
  s=$(psql -At -d "$SOURCE_URL" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM $t")
  d=$(psql -At -d "$TARGET_URL" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM $t")
  printf "%-12s source=%-10s target=%-10s %s\n" "$t" "$s" "$d" \
    "$([ "$s" = "$d" ] && echo OK || echo MISMATCH)"
done

psql -d "$TARGET_URL" -c "ANALYZE;"

Only after the application is healthy:

-- On the target
ALTER SUBSCRIPTION mig_sub DISABLE;
-- Later, once rollback is no longer an option:
DROP SUBSCRIPTION mig_sub;   -- also drops the slot on the source

Do not drop the subscription immediately — DROP SUBSCRIPTION removes the replication slot, and with it your cheap rollback.

Step 5: rollback

Two tiers, pick based on risk appetite.

Tier 1 — within the first minutes. The source is still intact and read-only. Revert the DSN, re-enable writes, scale back up:

psql -d "$SOURCE_URL" -c "ALTER DATABASE appdb SET default_transaction_read_only = off;"
# restore previous DSN in the secret store, then
oc annotate externalsecret/app-db -n app force-sync="$(date +%s)" --overwrite
oc rollout restart deploy/api -n app

Cost: you lose any writes already committed to the target. Acceptable only in the first minutes, which is why smoke tests must be fast and automated.

Tier 2 — reverse replication. Before re-opening writes, create a publication on the target and a subscription on the source with copy_data = false. Writes then flow back, and rollback becomes lossless for hours. This doubles the setup work and requires the reverse network path, but for a payments or ordering database it is worth it.

-- On the target (new primary)
CREATE PUBLICATION back_pub FOR ALL TABLES;
-- On the old source
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION back_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=appdb.abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com dbname=appdb user=repl sslmode=verify-full'
  PUBLICATION back_pub WITH (copy_data = false, slot_name = 'back_slot');

Remember to re-run the sequence sync in the reverse direction if you ever use it.

Security best practices

Dedicated replication role, least privilege. Do not reuse the application user. The source role needs only REPLICATION plus SELECT on replicated tables:

CREATE ROLE repl WITH LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD :'pw';
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE appdb TO repl;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO repl;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO repl;

Force TLS end to end. Logical replication streams plaintext row data. Use sslmode=verify-full with an explicit sslrootcert, never require (which does not verify the hostname). Set rds.force_ssl=1 / cloudsql requireSsl on the target, and hostssl only in the source pg_hba.conf:

hostssl appdb repl 10.42.0.0/16 scram-sha-256

Never put the DSN in a manifest. Use External Secrets, Vault, or at minimum a sealed secret. The CREATE SUBSCRIPTION connection string containing the password is stored in pg_subscription and visible to superusers — rotate that password right after cutover.

Restrict the network path. The source must only be reachable from the target's NAT egress IPs, and the migration Jobs must only reach the two databases:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-migration-egress
  namespace: data
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { job-name: pg-schema-bootstrap }
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.42.10.0/24 }   # source Postgres
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.43.20.0/24 }   # RDS subnet
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: openshift-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }

Harden the pods. The Job above runs runAsNonRoot, drops all capabilities and uses RuntimeDefault seccomp, so it passes the restricted-v2 SCC without exceptions. Never run migration tooling as a cluster-admin service account.

Keep an audit trail. Enable log_replication_commands = on on the source during the migration window, and snapshot the source (EBS snapshot / volume snapshot) immediately before the freeze. Replication is not a backup.

Key takeaways

  • Logical replication moves the expensive work out of the maintenance window. The only serialised steps are freeze, drain, sequences, switch — 2 to 5 minutes regardless of database size.
  • wal_level = logical is your only mandatory restart. Schedule it days ahead and the cutover itself needs no restart at all.
  • Replication slots are a loaded gun. They guarantee durability and they fill your source disk. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size, alert on retained WAL, and never leave an inactive slot behind.
  • Sequences and indexes are not replicated. Script the setval sync, and build secondary indexes after the initial copy with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
  • Monitor with pg_stat_replication and pg_stat_subscription, not with hope. Cut over only when the byte lag is literally zero.
  • Keep the subscription disabled, not dropped, for 24–48 hours. Dropping it destroys the slot and your fast rollback. For high-stakes data, invest in reverse replication before re-opening writes.
  • pglogical for old sources and sequence replication, DMS for heterogeneous migrations, native logical replication for everything else.

Rehearse the whole runbook against a restored snapshot first. The second time you execute it, five minutes will feel generous.

title: n8n Error Handling: One Error Workflow That Alerts You on Slack and Email (Without Spam)
summary:
If you run n8n in production, the scariest failure is the silent one. A webhook stops firing, a token expires, a Google Sheet changes shape, and nobody notices for a week.

n8n has a built in answer for this: the Error Trigger node and the Error workflow setting. This post shows a small error workflow that tells you exactly what broke, and does not flood your channel when the same workflow fails every minute.

How n8n error workflows work

  1. You build one workflow that starts with an Error Trigger node.
  2. In every workflow you want to watch, open Workflow settings > Error workflow and pick it.
  3. When a watched workflow fails during a production run, n8n starts your error workflow and passes it the details.

Two things trip people up:

  • Manual runs do not count. Error workflows run for production executions (triggers, schedules, webhooks), not when you click "Test workflow" in the editor. If your test "does nothing", that is why.
  • Activate it. Older docs said an error workflow does not need to be active. On the version I tested (n8n 2.48.7, self hosted) it only fired once it was active. Activating it costs nothing, so do it.

What the Error Trigger gives you

For a normal failure, the trigger output looks roughly like this:

{
  "execution": {
    "id": "231",
    "url": "https://your-n8n/workflow/12/executions/231",
    "error": { "message": "The resource you are requesting could not be found" },
    "lastNodeExecuted": "Get rows",
    "mode": "trigger"
  },
  "workflow": { "id": "12", "name": "Daily KPI report" }
}

If the failure happened in the trigger itself (for example a polling trigger with bad credentials), you get a trigger object instead of execution, and there is no execution URL. Handle both.

The workflow: 5 nodes

  1. Error Trigger
  2. Settings (Edit Fields): slack_channel, alert_email, quiet_minutes
  3. Build alert (Code): formats the message and drops repeats
  4. Alert on Slack
  5. Alert by email

Set both alert nodes to continue on error, so a broken Slack token does not also kill the email.

The Code node: readable alert plus flood control

Workflow static data persists between production runs, so we can remember which errors we already sent:

const data = $getWorkflowStaticData('global');
const settings = $('Settings').first().json;
const quietMs = (settings.quiet_minutes ?? 30) * 60 * 1000;

const exec = $json.execution;
const trig = $json.trigger;
const wf = $json.workflow ?? {};

const node = exec?.lastNodeExecuted ?? 'trigger';
const message = exec?.error?.message ?? trig?.error?.message ?? 'Unknown error';
const url = exec?.url ?? '(trigger error, no execution link)';

const key = `${wf.id}|${node}|${message}`;
const now = Date.now();
data.seen = data.seen ?? {};
const last = data.seen[key];

if (last && now - last.at < quietMs) {
  last.held = (last.held ?? 0) + 1;   // count it, send nothing
  return [];
}

const held = last?.held ?? 0;
data.seen[key] = { at: now, held: 0 };

let text = `🚨 n8n: "${wf.name}" failed at "${node}"\n${message}\n${url}`;
if (held) text += `\n(${held} identical errors were held back)`;

return [{ json: { text, subject: `n8n failure: ${wf.name}` } }];

Returning an empty array stops the run, so repeats inside the quiet period send nothing. The next alert after the quiet period says how many were skipped. Set quiet_minutes to 0 if you want every single error.

Static data is only saved for production runs, which is fine here because error workflows only run in production anyway.

Point your workflows at it

Open each workflow you care about, Workflow settings > Error workflow, pick this one, save. To test, add a node that always fails to a scratch workflow (an HTTP Request to a URL that returns 404), point it at the error workflow, activate it with a schedule trigger and let it run once.

What I would add next

  • A daily health report that lists failed executions of the last 24 hours, grouped by workflow, and the active workflows that still have no error workflow set (that list is the real gold: it shows what can fail silently).
  • Nightly backups of every workflow to a private GitHub repo, committing only real changes.

I packaged this alert workflow (with Slack and Gmail wired up and canvas notes), the daily health report and the GitHub backup as the n8n Ops Kit, tested on n8n 2.48.7: https://sarahstudiohq.gumroad.com/l/n8n-ops-kit

But the code above is the core of the alert, and it works on its own. If you have a better way to group repeated errors, I would like to hear it in the comments.

title: Test a Support Runbook With a Restricted Receiving Account
summary:
A support runbook can be accurate for its author and unusable for the receiving team. The commands may be correct. The missing assumption is often the account: the author inspected a resource with privileges that the receiving analyst will not have. A document review alone can miss that difference.

Rehearse the documented task with the intended receiving account before accepting the handover. Record each step's required capability, target resource and result. If a step cannot run, stop at that boundary and identify the missing prerequisite. An administrator's successful demonstration answers a different question from a restricted analyst's ability to follow the instructions.

The example below is an executable, in-memory capability model. Its controlled defect failed four of nine tests; the corrected path passed all nine. These observations concern the small Python model only. No cloud account, production permission, customer environment or real support action was used. The model helps make a runbook's assumptions explicit; it does not validate an organization's IAM configuration.

An AI agent prepared this tutorial and synthetic code and ran the local checks. Human manuscript review has not been performed. The reported observations concern the included in-memory fixture.

Give the receiving account a specific task

The fictional receiving analyst needs to inspect a diagnostic report and decide which authorized owner should handle a held job. The analyst can read the report. The analyst cannot retry the job. That boundary makes a useful rehearsal: the runbook must provide a complete diagnostic path without requiring the analyst to perform the restricted recovery action.

Name the account in the rehearsal material. In this example it is receiving-readonly. Its declared capabilities are read:report and read:absent. The second capability exists solely to exercise the distinction between permission to inspect a resource and the resource actually being present. These strings are local model values, not cloud permission names or credentials.

The synthetic resource map contains report and job. A report inspection has no modeled side effect. A retry appends an entry to an in-memory effects list. That list gives the tests something concrete to inspect when a step should have been denied. It is deliberately separate from the evidence list, which records attempted steps whether they complete or stop.

A useful runbook states what the analyst is expected to conclude from the report. If the next action requires a different owner, the diagnostic path should end with a handover to that owner. Silently assuming that the analyst can obtain broader privileges turns the instructions into a different operating procedure.

Controlled local execution: four failing checks, followed by nine passing checks.

Treat prerequisites as data the runner checks

Each step has a name, an action, a resource and a declared required capability. The model supports two actions: inspect requires a read capability, while retry requires a write capability. The runner derives the expected capability from the action and resource. It then checks that the declared capability matches the derived value.

That extra check matters. A step named retry must not acquire permission merely by declaring read:report as its prerequisite. Trusting the supplied capability label would allow the worksheet to authorize its own operation. The operation mapping is therefore part of the runner's fixed model, while the step declaration is input to validate.

The same principle appears in OWASP's authorization guidance under "Validate the Permissions on Every Request". In this example, each modeled step receives a fresh capability check. The quote supports the general authorization principle; it does not make this local runner a production security boundary.

After validating the declaration, the corrected runner checks the account's capability before checking whether the resource exists. A denied request therefore stops as DENIED. An authorized request for an absent resource stops as MISSING_RESOURCE. Correct the procedure before widening the account

A blocked step can reveal that the runbook assigned the wrong task to the receiving role. If the analyst submits only the final denial, it loses the permitted work already completed. The ordered evidence list carries both. That is why the runner records a status for the blocked step before it stops.

Make the next owner's request specific

A useful escalation can identify the runbook version, receiving role, blocked step and required capability, then ask for a defined decision. For the synthetic case, the request is whether the documented task should end with diagnosis or include an authorized retry by another role. The evidence supports asking that question; it does not settle the answer.

Attach the relevant resource reference and its access conditions through the organization's established channel. A receiving owner should know whether a link points to an actual retained observation, a changing dashboard or an example. This fixture supplies only synthetic data, so its public output can be reproduced without exposing an operational record.

Ask the next owner to preserve the disposition with the reviewed runbook. If the task remains diagnostic, revise the instructions to name the receiving evidence and escalation destination. If an additional action is accepted, state who performs it and which review or approval applies. Neither route requires the article's fixture to become a production authorization service.

Finally, define what would trigger another rehearsal. A changed operation, a different resource or a new receiving role can invalidate an earlier observation. Repeat the affected review rather than copying the previous passing result onto the revised procedure. Keeping that scope attached to the evidence makes a modest local exercise useful during later handovers.

Leave a reproducible receiving record

The practical deliverable is the reviewed runbook, the intended account boundary and the ordered evidence for the rehearsed steps. Retain the failed control alongside the passing correction when sharing this example. A reader can then reproduce why skipping the capability guard changes the outcome instead of relying on an unsupported assertion that access was checked.

For a real handover, keep the environment, applicable runbook version and unresolved prerequisites with that record. Repeat the relevant review when one of those assumptions changes. The procedure becomes reviewable when the receiving team can show what it could inspect, where it had to stop and who owns the next authorized decision.

title: Does an AI agent's task keep running after you close the chat?
summary:
Disclosure: I work on CMDOP, the tool I use as the example here.

You ask an agent to run a long build or a test suite on your machine, then you close the chat. Did the job die with it? With most setups the honest answer is "it depends on how the command was started", and people end up wrapping everything in tmux just to be sure.

Here is how it works in CMDOP, including the cases where a task does stop.

The task lives on the computer, not in the chat

A long task runs in a real terminal on your computer and gets an id straight away. The chat is only the place where you asked for it. Close the chat and the task is still there.

When you come back, the agent reads the task's output like a screen, whether it is still running or already finished, and it can stop the task by its id. The computer keeps the output of its last 50 tasks.

What actually stops a task

Three things, and it is worth knowing all of them before you rely on a long run:

  1. You stop it by its id.
  2. You pause the computer. Pause stops every tool call on that computer and its running tasks, and only a person sitting at the computer can resume it.
  3. The CMDOP program on that computer restarts, which includes an update. Running tasks do not survive that. Afterwards they are listed as lost, so you know to start them again instead of waiting for output that will never come.

A simple routine

  • Ask the agent to start the long job as a task and to tell you its id.
  • Close the chat and do something else.
  • Later, ask the agent to read that task's output by its id.
  • If the program restarted in between, expect the task to show as lost and start it again.

One more thing: running commands is not on by default. A new agent can only read until you switch running on for that agent yourself.

How do you keep long agent jobs alive today: tmux, a separate server, or something else?

title: Backing up self-hosted n8n: what to save, how often, and how to prove a restore works
summary:
Self-hosting n8n is cheap and flexible, but it moves one job from the vendor to you: backups. Most small teams I work with have something in place, usually a snapshot of the whole server. That helps, but it often isn't enough to get a single broken workflow back quickly, and nobody has ever tested whether the snapshot actually restores.

This is the backup routine I set up for small teams running n8n in Docker. It's boring on purpose.

1. Know what actually needs saving

An n8n instance has four things you care about:

  1. The database. Workflows, credentials (encrypted), execution history and settings live here. On small installs this is often SQLite inside the n8n data folder; on larger ones it's Postgres.
  2. The encryption key. Credentials in the database are encrypted with N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY (or the key n8n generated on first start and stored in its config file). Lose the key and your restored credentials are useless.
  3. Your environment and compose files. The docker-compose.yml, the .env file and any reverse-proxy config. Without these, rebuilding takes hours of guessing.
  4. Files your workflows write to disk, if any (exports, generated PDFs, uploaded files).

If you only take one thing from this post: store the encryption key somewhere separate from the server, such as a password manager. A backup of the database without the key is half a backup.

2. Two layers: whole-server and per-workflow

I use two layers because they solve different problems.

Layer 1: nightly file-level backup of the data folder and database. For SQLite, stop writes or use the SQLite backup command so you don't copy a file mid-write. For Postgres, a nightly pg_dump is simple and reliable. Push the result off the server to object storage with a tool that does encryption and versioning (Kopia, Restic and Borg are all fine). Keep at least 14 days, longer if the storage is cheap.

Layer 2: workflow exports to Git. The n8n CLI can export workflows as JSON:

docker exec n8n n8n export:workflow --all --separate --output=/home/node/backup/workflows

Commit that folder to a private repository once a day. Now when someone "improves" a workflow on Friday afternoon and breaks it, you can diff Thursday's version and paste it back in minutes, without touching the database.

Credentials can be exported too, but only decrypted or encrypted with the instance key. I keep credential exports out of Git and rely on Layer 1 plus the stored key.

3. Schedule it, then alert on failure

Run both layers from cron or a systemd timer, not from inside n8n itself. If n8n is down, a backup workflow inside n8n is down with it.

Every backup job should end by reporting success somewhere a human will notice its absence. A simple pattern: the job pings a heartbeat URL (a monitoring service, or a small webhook) and that service alerts you if the ping doesn't arrive for 26 hours. Alerting on silence catches the failure mode that matters most: the backup that quietly stopped running weeks ago.

4. Test a restore every quarter

A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a backup. Once a quarter:

  1. Start a throwaway VM or a local Docker host.
  2. Restore the compose files, .env and the latest database dump.
  3. Set the same encryption key and start n8n.
  4. Log in, open three important workflows, and run one manually against a test endpoint.
  5. Write down how long it took and anything you had to look up.

The first test usually reveals something: a missing environment variable, a reverse-proxy setting nobody documented, a webhook URL hard-coded to the old hostname. Fixing those on a quiet Tuesday is much better than discovering them during an outage.

5. Watch the execution history size

Execution data is often the biggest part of the database. Keep enough history to debug (I like at least two weeks), but turn on pruning so the database doesn't grow forever and backups stay fast. Check the variables for execution data pruning and max age in your n8n version's docs and set them explicitly rather than trusting defaults.

6. A one-page runbook

Finally, write a single page that says:

  • where backups are stored and how to access them,
  • where the encryption key is,
  • the exact restore commands,
  • who to call.

Put it next to the server documentation, not on the server.

Summary

  • Back up the database, the encryption key, the config files and any written files.
  • Use a nightly off-site backup plus daily workflow exports to Git.
  • Run backups outside n8n and alert when they don't report in.
  • Test a full restore quarterly and keep a one-page runbook.

If you're moving to self-hosted n8n and want this set up properly from day one, I describe how I handle it on my n8n automation services page. If you're still on Zapier, my notes on a self-hosted Zapier to n8n migration cover what to inventory before you move.

title: The DevOps Toolchain Explained: Which Tools to Learn, What Each One Solves, and How They Fit Together
summary:
Open any DevOps job listing and you'll see a wall of tool names: Git, Jenkins, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Prometheus, and a long list of cloud services. For a beginner, the list reads like a shopping list with no instructions. The more useful question is what problem each tool solves, because once you see that, the order in which to learn them becomes clear.

Tools only make sense when you see how they connect. A commit triggers a build, the build produces a container, the container runs on infrastructure defined in code, and monitoring watches the result. Learners who follow a devops full course, or who put together an equivalent plan on their own, tend to do best when each tool is introduced alongside the problem it fixes, instead of as an isolated topic to memorise.

This article walks through the DevOps toolchain layer by layer, explains what each category does, names the common options, and shows how to practise each one.

The DevOps Toolchain at a Glance

A toolchain is the set of tools that carries software from an idea to a running, monitored service. Most teams organise it around a loop: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, and monitor. Each stage has tools that automate it, and the feedback from monitoring flows back into planning.

Here is the simplified map used throughout this article:

  • Source control: Git and GitHub
  • Build and delivery: Jenkins and other CI/CD tools
  • Packaging: Docker
  • Orchestration: Kubernetes
  • Infrastructure: AWS with Terraform
  • Configuration: Ansible
  • Observability: Prometheus and Grafana

You don't need every tool in every category. You need to understand each category and be competent with one representative tool in it.

Foundations: Linux, Networking, and Scripting

Before any named tool, there is a layer of fundamentals that nearly every tool assumes. Linux is the operating system under most servers and containers, so command-line navigation, permissions, processes, and package management matter. Networking basics, including IP addressing, DNS, ports, and HTTP, help you diagnose why services can't reach each other. Bash scripting lets you automate repetitive work, and a little Python is a common complement.

These aren't glamorous, but they are the difference between running a tool and understanding it. When a container fails to start or a pipeline step errors out, the explanation is usually a Linux or networking detail.

Git and GitHub: The Source of Truth

Git is a distributed version control system that records every change to your code and configuration. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket host repositories and add collaboration features such as pull requests and code review. Version control matters in DevOps because it is the trigger for everything else: pipelines run when code changes, and infrastructure definitions live in repositories too.

To build competence, practise branching, merging, resolving conflicts, and opening pull requests on a small project. Learn a simple branching strategy so you can explain how a change moves from a feature branch to production.

CI/CD: Jenkins and Its Alternatives

Continuous integration (CI) means merging code frequently and verifying each change with an automated build and tests. Continuous delivery or deployment (CD) extends that to releasing the verified build. Together, a CI/CD pipeline replaces manual, error-prone release steps with a repeatable process.

Jenkins is a widely used, self-hosted automation server that is a good way to learn pipeline concepts: stages, agents, triggers, credentials, and artifacts. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and similar tools express the same ideas in different syntax. Because the concepts transfer, it is more valuable to understand how a pipeline is structured than to memorise one product's interface. A good exercise is a pipeline that checks out code, runs tests, builds an image, and deploys to a test environment.

Docker: Packaging Applications Consistently

Docker packages an application and its dependencies into a container image that runs the same way on any machine with a container runtime. It tackles the "works on my machine" problem by making the environment part of the artifact.

Focus on the building blocks: writing a Dockerfile, understanding image layers, mapping ports, using volumes for persistent data, and connecting containers with networks. Docker Compose is a natural next step for running a small multi-container application, such as a web service with a database. Learn to keep images small and avoid baking secrets into them.

Kubernetes: Running Containers at Scale

One container is easy to run. Dozens across several machines need scheduling, networking, scaling, and recovery, and Kubernetes provides that. It runs groups of containers as pods, manages them through deployments, exposes them with services, and replaces failed instances automatically.

Kubernetes has a steep vocabulary, so learn it after Docker. Local environments such as minikube or kind let you practise without cloud costs. Start with deployments, services, config maps, and secrets, then explore rolling updates and basic troubleshooting with commands like kubectl describe and kubectl logs. Helm, a package manager for Kubernetes, becomes useful once you are comfortable with the basics.

Cloud Platforms: AWS as a Starting Point

Cloud providers supply compute, storage, networking, and managed services on demand. AWS is a common starting point, though Azure and Google Cloud follow similar principles, so skills transfer. For DevOps work, prioritise these AWS services:

  • IAM for identities, roles, and permissions.
  • EC2 for virtual servers, with security groups and load balancers.
  • VPC for networking, subnets, route tables, and gateways.
  • S3 for object storage.
  • CloudWatch for metrics, logs, and alarms.

Treat security as part of the lesson. Understanding least-privilege IAM policies early will save you from habits that are hard to unlearn.

Terraform and Ansible: Infrastructure as Code

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining infrastructure in version-controlled files instead of clicking through a console. Terraform is a declarative provisioning tool: you describe the resources you want, such as a VPC, servers, and a load balancer, and it works out how to create or change them. It tracks what it manages in a state file, which is an important concept to understand, including why state should be stored remotely and protected.

Ansible handles configuration management. Using playbooks written in YAML, it connects to servers over SSH to install packages, manage files, and start services. A useful rule of thumb is that Terraform creates the infrastructure and Ansible configures what runs on it, though the two overlap in some cases. Practise by provisioning a small environment with Terraform, then configuring it with an Ansible playbook, and destroying and recreating it to prove repeatability.

Prometheus and Grafana: Seeing What Is Happening

Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs, typically metrics, logs, and traces. Prometheus scrapes and stores metrics and supports alerting rules, while Grafana turns those metrics into dashboards. Log aggregation tools, such as the ELK stack or Loki, help you search events across services.

The skill here goes beyond installing the tools. Learn to decide what to measure, such as request rate, error rate, and latency, and to write alerts that point to real problems. An alert that fires constantly teaches a team to ignore it.

How the Tools Work Together: A Worked Example

Imagine a small web application. A developer opens a pull request on GitHub. A Jenkins pipeline runs tests, builds a Docker image, and pushes it to a registry. Terraform has already provisioned the AWS network and a Kubernetes cluster, and Ansible configured any supporting servers. The pipeline updates the Kubernetes deployment, which rolls out new pods gradually. Prometheus tracks error rates and latency, Grafana displays them, and an alert notifies the team if the release degrades. If it does, a rollback restores the previous image.

No single tool does all of this. The value comes from the connections, which is why practising them together matters more than collecting certificates for each.

Choosing and Learning Tools Without Overload

A few principles keep the toolchain manageable. Learn one tool per category before exploring alternatives. Follow the order of dependency: Linux and Git, then scripting and CI/CD, then Docker, cloud, Kubernetes, IaC, and observability. Build a small project at each stage so each new tool has a purpose. Read official documentation as you go, since it stays current when tutorials age.

Some learners prefer a guided path with scheduled sessions and feedback. An instructor-led DevOps training program is one way to get that sequence and hands-on practice, while others assemble their own plan from documentation and projects. Either approach works if it keeps you building things.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which DevOps tools should I learn first?
Begin with Linux and Git, then scripting, CI/CD, and Docker. Cloud, Kubernetes, and Infrastructure as Code follow naturally.

Do I need to learn every tool in the DevOps toolchain?
No. Understand each category and become proficient with one representative tool in it. The concepts transfer between tools.

What is the difference between Terraform and Ansible?
Terraform provisions infrastructure such as networks and servers, while Ansible configures software and settings on machines that already exist.

Should I learn Docker before Kubernetes?
Yes. Kubernetes orchestrates containers, so understanding images, containers, and networking first makes its concepts far easier.

Is Jenkins still worth learning?
It remains widely used and teaches pipeline fundamentals that apply to GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and others.

Which cloud platform should a beginner choose?

event_model_payload.summary:
Open any DevOps job listing and you'll see a wall of tool names: Git, Jenkins, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Prometheus, and a long list of cloud services. For a beginner, the list reads like a shopping list with no instructions. The more useful question is what problem each tool solves, because once you see that, the order in which to learn them becomes clear.

Tools only make sense when you see how they connect. A commit triggers a build, the build produces a container, the container runs on infrastructure defined in code, and monitoring watches the result. Learners who follow a devops full course, or who put together an equivalent plan on their own, tend to do best when each tool is introduced alongside the problem it fixes, instead of as an isolated topic to memorise.

This article walks through the DevOps toolchain layer by layer, explains what each category does, names the common options, and shows how to practise each one.

The DevOps Toolchain at a Glance

A toolchain is the set of tools that carries software from an idea to a running, monitored service. Most teams organise it around a loop: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, and monitor. Each stage has tools that automate it, and the feedback from monitoring flows back into planning.

Here is the simplified map used throughout this article:

  • Source control: Git and GitHub
  • Build and delivery: Jenkins and other CI/CD tools
  • Packaging: Docker
  • Orchestration: Kubernetes
  • Infrastructure: AWS with Terraform
  • Configuration: Ansible
  • Observability: Prometheus and Grafana

You don't need every tool in every category. You need to understand each category and be competent with one representative tool in it.

Foundations: Linux, Networking, and Scripting

Before any named tool, there is a layer of fundamentals that nearly every tool assumes. Linux is the operating system under most servers and containers, so command-line navigation, permissions, processes, and package management matter. Networking basics, including IP addressing, DNS, ports, and HTTP, help you diagnose why services can't reach each other. Bash scripting lets you automate repetitive work, and a little Python is a common complement.

These aren't glamorous, but they are the difference between running a tool and understanding it. When a container fails to start or a pipeline step errors out, the explanation is usually a Linux or networking detail.

Git and GitHub: The Source of Truth

Git is a distributed version control system that records every change to your code and configuration. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket host repositories and add collaboration features such as pull requests and code review. Version control matters in DevOps because it is the trigger for everything else: pipelines run when code changes, and infrastructure definitions live in repositories too.

To build competence, practise branching, merging, resolving conflicts, and opening pull requests on a small project. Learn a simple branching strategy so you can explain how a change moves from a feature branch to production.

CI/CD: Jenkins and Its Alternatives

Continuous integration (CI) means merging code frequently and verifying each change with an automated build and tests. Continuous delivery or deployment (CD) extends that to releasing the verified build. Together, a CI/CD pipeline replaces manual, error-prone release steps with a repeatable process.

Jenkins is a widely used, self-hosted automation server that is a good way to learn pipeline concepts: stages, agents, triggers, credentials, and artifacts. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and similar tools express the same ideas in different syntax. Because the concepts transfer, it is more valuable to understand how a pipeline is structured than to memorise one product's interface. A good exercise is a pipeline that checks out code, runs tests, builds an image, and deploys to a test environment.

Docker: Packaging Applications Consistently

Docker packages an application and its dependencies into a container image that runs the same way on any machine with a container runtime. It tackles the "works on my machine" problem by making the environment part of the artifact.

Focus on the building blocks: writing a Dockerfile, understanding image layers, mapping ports, using volumes for persistent data, and connecting containers with networks. Docker Compose is a natural next step for running a small multi-container application, such as a web service with a database. Learn to keep images small and avoid baking secrets into them.

Kubernetes: Running Containers at Scale

One container is easy to run. Dozens across several machines need scheduling, networking, scaling, and recovery, and Kubernetes provides that. It runs groups of containers as pods, manages them through deployments, exposes them with services, and replaces failed instances automatically.

Kubernetes has a steep vocabulary, so learn it after Docker. Local environments such as minikube or kind let you practise without cloud costs. Start with deployments, services, config maps, and secrets, then explore rolling updates and basic troubleshooting with commands like kubectl describe and kubectl logs. Helm, a package manager for Kubernetes, becomes useful once you are comfortable with the basics.

Cloud Platforms: AWS as a Starting Point

Cloud providers supply compute, storage, networking, and managed services on demand. AWS is a common starting point, though Azure and Google Cloud follow similar principles, so skills transfer. For DevOps work, prioritise these AWS services:

  • IAM for identities, roles, and permissions.
  • EC2 for virtual servers, with security groups and load balancers.
  • VPC for networking, subnets, route tables, and gateways.
  • S3 for object storage.
  • CloudWatch for metrics, logs, and alarms.

Treat security as part of the lesson. Understanding least-privilege IAM policies early will save you from habits that are hard to unlearn.

Terraform and Ansible: Infrastructure as Code

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining infrastructure in version-controlled files instead of clicking through a console. Terraform is a declarative provisioning tool: you describe the resources you want, such as a VPC, servers, and a load balancer, and it works out how to create or change them. It tracks what it manages in a state file, which is an important concept to understand, including why state should be stored remotely and protected.

Ansible handles configuration management. Using playbooks written in YAML, it connects to servers over SSH to install packages, manage files, and start services. A useful rule of thumb is that Terraform creates the infrastructure and Ansible configures what runs on it, though the two overlap in some cases. Practise by provisioning a small environment with Terraform, then configuring it with an Ansible playbook, and destroying and recreating it to prove repeatability.

Prometheus and Grafana: Seeing What Is Happening

Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs, typically metrics, logs, and traces. Prometheus scrapes and stores metrics and supports alerting rules, while Grafana turns those metrics into dashboards. Log aggregation tools, such as the ELK stack or Loki, help you search events across services.

The skill here goes beyond installing the tools. Learn to decide what to measure, such as request rate, error rate, and latency, and to write alerts that point to real problems. An alert that fires constantly teaches a team to ignore it.

How the Tools Work Together: A Worked Example

Imagine a small web application. A developer opens a pull request on GitHub. A Jenkins pipeline runs tests, builds a Docker image, and pushes it to a registry. Terraform has already provisioned the AWS network and a Kubernetes cluster, and Ansible configured any supporting servers. The pipeline updates the Kubernetes deployment, which rolls out new pods gradually. Prometheus tracks error rates and latency, Grafana displays them, and an alert notifies the team if the release degrades. If it does, a rollback restores the previous image.

No single tool does all of this. The value comes from the connections, which is why practising them together matters more than collecting certificates for each.

Choosing and Learning Tools Without Overload

A few principles keep the toolchain manageable. Learn one tool per category before exploring alternatives. Follow the order of dependency: Linux and Git, then scripting and CI/CD, then Docker, cloud, Kubernetes, IaC, and observability. Build a small project at each stage so each new tool has a purpose. Read official documentation as you go, since it stays current when tutorials age.

Some learners prefer a guided path with scheduled sessions and feedback. An instructor-led DevOps training program is one way to get that sequence and hands-on practice, while others assemble their own plan from documentation and projects. Either approach works if it keeps you building things.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which DevOps tools should I learn first?
Begin with Linux and Git, then scripting, CI/CD, and Docker. Cloud, Kubernetes, and Infrastructure as Code follow naturally.

Do I need to learn every tool in the DevOps toolchain?
No. Understand each category and become proficient with one representative tool in it. The concepts transfer between tools.

What is the difference between Terraform and Ansible?
Terraform provisions infrastructure such as networks and servers, while Ansible configures software and settings on machines that already exist.

Should I learn Docker before Kubernetes?
Yes. Kubernetes orchestrates containers, so understanding images, containers, and networking first makes its concepts far easier.

Is Jenkins still worth learning?
It remains widely used and teaches pipeline fundamentals that apply to GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and others.

Which cloud platform should a beginner choose?
AWS is a common choice because of its market presence and documentation, but the core ideas carry over to Azure and Google Cloud.

Putting the Toolchain Together

The DevOps toolchain looks intimidating only when you view it as a list. Seen as a pipeline from commit to monitored production service, each tool has a clear job. Learn the fundamentals, add one tool at a time, connect them through small projects, and let troubleshooting teach you what documentation can't.

title: How to Run Zero-Downtime Database Migrations
summary:
Most database migration failures happen because we try to move too fast.

A developer needs to change a schema, update the application code, and backfill existing rows. To save time, they bundle everything into a single deployment step: the migration alters the column, the new app code deploys immediately after, and an update script runs against the live database.

In production environments running rolling updates, Kubernetes pods, or serverless instances, this single-step approach breaks. While the deployment rolls out, version 1 of your application (which expects the old schema) and version 2 (which expects the new schema) run at the same time. If version 2 immediately renames or drops a column, version 1 crashes. If the data backfill locks a massive table, the entire API hangs.

The result is usually a 2 AM emergency rollback and a corrupted or half-migrated database.

To achieve zero downtime, database migrations must be decoupled from code deployments using a structured design pattern.

The Solution: Expand and Contract

The Expand-and-Contract pattern (also known as Parallel Change) breaks schema changes into incremental, backward-compatible steps. The fundamental rule is simple: old and new versions of your application must always be able to run simultaneously without error.

Instead of executing a schema change in one deployment, you break it into three distinct phases.

1. The Expand Phase

First, modify the database schema by adding new columns or tables alongside the old ones. Do not delete, rename, or add NOT NULL constraints without default values to existing fields yet.

-- Step 1: Expand
-- Add the new column, keeping it nullable so old application writes don't fail.
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name VARCHAR(255);

At this stage, existing application instances continue writing to and reading from first_name and last_name. The database update is completely invisible to live traffic.

2. Dual-Writing and Data Backfilling

Next, deploy application code that writes to both the old and new columns whenever a record is updated or created.

Once dual-writing is live, backfill historical records. Never run a single massive UPDATE statement on a large table in production, as this causes heavy lock contention. Instead, process data in small background batches.

# Step 2: Batch Backfill Script
import time

def backfill_full_name(batch_size=1000):
    while True:
        # Update records in small chunks to avoid locking the database table
        query = """
            WITH target_rows AS (
                SELECT id FROM users
                WHERE full_name IS NULL
                LIMIT :batch_size
            )
            UPDATE users
            SET full_name = CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)
            FROM target_rows
            WHERE users.id = target_rows.id;
        """
        result = db.execute(query, {"batch_size": batch_size})

        # Stop when no remaining rows need backfilling
        if result.rowcount == 0:
            break

        time.sleep(0.1)  # Throttle backfill to keep I/O low

3. The Switch and Contract Phase

Once all historical data is backfilled and both fields remain in sync:

  1. Deploy a new version of the application that reads directly from the new full_name column while continuing to write to both (or just the new column).
  2. Verify that old instances of the application are fully decommissioned.
  3. Remove references to the old columns from the application codebase entirely.
  4. Execute the final cleanup migration to drop the old fields. 
-- Step 3: Contract
-- Safe to execute only after no active code touches these columns.
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN first_name;
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN last_name;

Separate Migrations from Application Startup

Another common operational mistake is executing database migrations directly inside the application startup command (e.g., inside a Docker container's ENTRYPOINT or CMD).

When scaling services horizontally across multiple containers or instances, every container booting at the same time attempts to execute schema changes simultaneously. This leads to race conditions, deadlocks, and failed container boots.

Instead, execute migrations as a dedicated, single-execution pipeline step in your CI/CD process before deploying new application containers. This ensures schema adjustments occur sequentially in a controlled environment.

By combining the expand-and-contract pattern with isolated CI/CD deployment steps, schema changes transform from high-risk production events into routine background updates.

title: Choosing a Jira Server Replacement for an Air-Gapped Environment
summary:
Replacing Jira Server in an air-gapped environment involves more than choosing an issue tracker. Installation, licensing, updates, integrations, and maintenance must all fit the isolation rules. You also need to decide which historical records and workflows to preserve—and how much process redesign is acceptable.

This guide compares seven options across those concerns. Use it to narrow the shortlist, then validate each candidate against representative projects and your offline operating procedures.
