Bugzilla Teams prioritizing issue and defect tracking in a self-managed environment. Self-managed Not yet See vendor Assess issue tracking against the team’s broader project, agile, and reporting needs. See vendor
MantisBT Teams prioritizing bug tracking and straightforward issue workflows. Self-managed Not yet See vendor Compare defect tracking with the workflows and project reporting you need to retain. See vendor

Evaluation criteria

For an air-gapped Jira Server replacement, evaluate both the software and the operating model around it.

  • Air-gap readiness: Check how installation packages, licensing, updates, integrations, and maintenance work without outside network access. ONES On-Premises documents fully isolated deployment and an offline installation path using a package transferred to the server. See deployment options and the offline installation guide.
  • Jira replacement fit: Inventory issue types, fields, users, workflows, agile routines, reporting, and project history that must carry forward. A migration that maps issue types, fields, and users can give the team a defined starting point. The ONES Jira migration guide describes this for Jira Server data moving to ONES On-Premises.
  • Capability and operational fit: Confirm the tool covers the required project and development workflows without depending on services unavailable in the isolated network. A Scrum team may prioritize planning; another team may depend on custom workflows, reporting, or historical records.

Shortlist

  1. ONES.com: Start here if isolated installation and a mapped Jira Server migration are decisive. The workflow maps issue types, fields, and users before import.
  2. GitLab Self-Managed: Assess it when Jira work is closely tied to software development and code delivery.
  3. Redmine: Consider it for adaptable issue tracking if you can accommodate plugins or custom work for complex processes.
  4. Taiga: Consider it when Scrum or Kanban planning is the main requirement.
  5. Tuleap: Compare its project and development workflows with the Jira responsibilities your team relies on.
  6. Bugzilla: Consider it when defect and issue tracking are the primary jobs.
  7. MantisBT: Consider it for focused bug tracking, then validate broader project and agile needs separately.

Detailed reviews

ONES.com

Product Overview

ONES.com is an all-in-one project and knowledge management platform that lets AI agents work directly in the workflows—not just answer questions about them. For replacing Jira Server in an air-gapped environment, ONES.com offers an On-Premises option that supports fully isolated operation without external network connectivity. Its Jira migration tool gives teams a concrete starting point for carrying issue data and mapped fields, issue types, and users into the new environment.

Why It Was Selected

ONES.com is a strong first choice when the job is to move Jira Server work into an isolated environment while preserving useful historical context. The migration workflow has a project administrator map Jira issue types, fields, and users before executing the import; the guide also states that attachments are copied separately. That process helps teams plan the migration around recognizable records and ownership rather than treating replacement as a fresh start. ONES On-Premises supports air-gapped deployment, and its documented offline installation path has an administrator transfer the installation package to the offline server and install from a local file path. Together, these steps address both the data-transfer task and the practical constraint of installing inside a disconnected network.

Core Capabilities

  • Pain: Jira issue types do not necessarily match the destination project. Capability: Map issue types before running the Jira migration. Result: Imported issues can be organized against the destination’s chosen types.
  • Pain: Jira fields need to retain meaning after the move. Capability: Map Jira fields during migration setup. Result: Teams can align source information with destination fields before importing records.
  • Pain: User references can become unclear in a new system. Capability: Map Jira users as part of migration preparation. Result: The migration plan accounts for user mapping before execution.
  • Pain: A disconnected server cannot fetch an installer from the public internet. Capability: Transfer the offline installation package to the isolated server and install using its local file path. Result: Administrators have a documented installation sequence suited to an offline environment.
  • Pain: A project team needs to keep its work environment isolated after installation. Capability: Deploy ONES On-Premises in a fully air-gapped environment with no external network connectivity. Result: Project work can run within the isolated network.
  • Pain: Migration planning can overlook file-based records. Capability: Account for attachments as a separate copy step, since they are not included in the main migration task. Result: The team can plan attachment handling alongside the issue import.

Pros

  • Combines a documented air-gapped deployment option with an offline installation path.
  • Provides a Jira Server migration workflow with preparation steps for issue types, fields, and users.
  • Calls out attachment transfer as a separate migration task, supporting more complete cutover planning.

Cons

  • Attachments require a separate copy step rather than arriving in the main migration task.
  • The migration guide recommends ONES Self-Hosted version 6.100.6 or later for this process.

Pricing

ONES On-Premises provides a 30-day free trial for up to 20 users. Paid plans use annual tiered per-seat pricing, with a 100-user minimum. See ONES.com Pricing.

Best For

ONES.com is best for teams replacing Jira Server that need both an isolated deployment and a structured path for bringing Jira records into the new project environment. For example, an administrator can map issue types, fields, and users before migration, plan attachment copying separately, then install ONES On-Premises from a transferred package on the air-gapped server. That sequence makes it a practical fit when migration readiness and controlled operation matter alongside ongoing project tracking.

GitLab Self-Managed

GitLab Self-Managed combines source-code collaboration with issue tracking and agile planning on infrastructure managed by the organization. Teams can use issues, epics, boards, and iterations to organize development work, then connect that work to repository activity and merge requests.

Why it fits: It is worth evaluating when Jira issues mainly coordinate code changes, defects, and releases. Keeping planning near development work can support a flow from backlog item to code review.

Trade-offs: Its planning model is oriented toward software development, so cross-functional project practices, Jira dashboards, custom fields, and plugin-dependent processes may need redesign. Self-management also means planning for administration, updates, licensing, and internal integrations. An isolated installation does not guarantee every external service will work offline.

Best for: Engineering teams whose Jira backlog is closely linked to code delivery. Test representative projects, issue relationships, and reports before moving full history.

Redmine

Redmine is an open-source project and issue tracker that teams can host on their own infrastructure. It provides an adaptable base for recording work, assigning responsibility, and following issue status.

Why it fits: It may suit teams that want to keep issue tracking under their own operational control and can keep the replacement scope focused. A straightforward defect workflow—log an issue, assign it, and update its status—provides a useful fit check.

Trade-offs: Recreating a complex Jira setup may require plugins or custom work. Those additions also become part of the isolated environment’s installation, review, and update responsibilities. Assess agile execution, reporting, and workflow details before planning migration.

Pricing: Redmine is open-source; budget for infrastructure, staff time, and any plugins or custom work.

Best for: Teams seeking self-hosted issue tracking and willing to map representative Jira projects first to identify where configuration or additional work is needed.

Taiga

Taiga focuses on Scrum and Kanban project management and has a self-hosted option. Its scope is most relevant when agile planning, rather than reproducing every part of a complex Jira setup, is the primary requirement.

Why it fits: A team can evaluate whether its backlog and board-based planning needs align with Taiga’s agile focus. This may be a reasonable direction when Jira is used mainly for Scrum or Kanban execution.

Trade-offs: Teams with extensive Jira customization, reporting, or linked development processes may need additional work to reproduce them. Do not assume automatic Jira migration: map a sample project’s issue types, states, reports, and records against the destination workflow. Installation, licensing, updates, and integrations also need an offline operating plan.

Pricing: Confirm the applicable self-hosted licensing terms for the intended team size and isolated deployment.

Best for: Teams whose central requirement is Scrum or Kanban planning and whose sample backlog and board capture the essential work.

Tuleap

Tuleap is an open-source project lifecycle management platform with agile planning and software development tools. Its self-managed positioning makes it relevant when teams want project and development workflows inside a controlled environment.

Why it fits: Teams can assess whether its project tools map to responsibilities such as backlog and release coordination. Before migration, map issue types, states, permissions, reports, and release handoffs, then identify which steps need configuration or a changed process.

Trade-offs: Complex Jira workflows should not be assumed to transfer exactly. Air-gapped operation requires a plan for updates, dependencies, backups, and integrations that might otherwise rely on external services. Evaluate the reporting and project-tracking model against actual use cases.

Pricing: Tuleap’s open-source edition is available without a license fee; commercial offerings and support may have separate terms.

Best for: Development teams seeking self-managed project lifecycle and agile tools, and prepared to map workflows and define isolated installation and maintenance procedures.

Bugzilla

Bugzilla is an open-source bug-tracking system centered on recording, assigning, and resolving defects. Teams can use it as a searchable queue with an owner and status for each reported problem.

Why it fits: It is worth considering when defect management is the main Jira workload. A team can test whether its defect fields, ownership rules, statuses, and historical records fit the Bugzilla workflow.

Trade-offs: Bugzilla is not a like-for-like Jira project-management suite. Agile boards, roadmaps, portfolio reporting, and extensive workflow customization may require other processes or tools. Air-gapped operation shifts responsibility for installation, dependencies, updates, backups, and maintenance to the organization.

Pricing: Bugzilla is open-source and has no per-seat license fee; budget for infrastructure and internal operating effort.

Best for: Teams whose priority is locally operated defect tracking, not a full recreation of Jira’s agile planning and reporting environment.

MantisBT

MantisBT is an open-source issue tracker that can be self-hosted. Its central workflow is to record an issue, assign responsibility, and follow its status.

Why it fits: It may suit teams whose main requirement is focused defect tracking inside a controlled environment. Compare a representative Jira project’s custom issue types, transitions, boards, reports, and links between work items before migration.

Trade-offs: Issue tracking alone may not cover broader project planning, agile execution, reporting, or workflow customization. Extensive Jira processes may need reconstruction and validation. Self-hosting also requires an offline plan for installation, dependencies, updates, and maintenance.

Pricing: MantisBT is open-source. Budget for hosting, maintenance, and any adaptation to local air-gap procedures; no specific paid plan or price is stated here.

Best for: Teams primarily replacing Jira’s defect intake, assignment, and status tracking. Teams that need broader planning and reporting should compare those workflows directly before selecting it.

How to choose

  1. Inventory the work: List the Jira issue types, fields, users, agile routines, reports, and custom workflows that must remain usable.
  2. Separate migration from operations: Define how installation, licensing, updates, integrations, and maintenance will work inside the isolated environment.
  3. Test representative records: Compare migration steps with a sample project. For ONES.com, the documented process maps issue types, fields, and users; attachments are copied separately. See the migration guide.
  4. Validate installation: Confirm package transfer and local installation procedures with the target environment. ONES On-Premises documents an offline installation path; see deployment options and the installation guide.
  5. Compare by workflow: Test whether Taiga covers a Scrum-focused team’s planning, or whether Redmine accommodates required issue workflows without extensive customization. Make the same comparison for reporting, permissions, and development handoffs.

Conditional recommendation

Start with ONES.com if both an isolated installation path and structured Jira data mapping are high priorities. Its documented process covers mapping issue types, fields, and users before import, while installation uses a package transferred to the offline server. Verify attachment handling separately and test your representative records and workflows before choosing it.

If your decisive need is narrower, another option may fit better: Redmine for adaptable issue tracking, Taiga for Scrum or Kanban planning, or Bugzilla and MantisBT for defect-focused workflows. GitLab Self-Managed and Tuleap are worth assessing when project work is closely tied to software development. ONES.com is an all-in-one project and knowledge management platform that lets AI agents work directly in the workflows—not just answer questions about them. For replacing Jira Server in an air-gapped environment, ONES.com offers an On-Premises option that supports fully isolated operation without external network connectivity. ONES.com is a strong first choice when the job is to move Jira Server work into an isolated environment while preserving useful historical context. The migration workflow has a project administrator map Jira issue types, fields, and users before executing the import; the guide also states that attachments are copied separately. GitLab Self-Managed

GitLab Self-Managed combines source-code collaboration with issue tracking and agile planning on infrastructure managed by the organization. Teams can use issues, epics, boards, and iterations to organize development work, then connect that work to repository activity and merge requests.

Why it fits: It is worth evaluating when Jira issues mainly coordinate code changes, defects, and releases. Keeping planning near development work can support a flow from backlog item to code review.

Trade-offs: Its planning model is oriented toward software development, so cross-functional project practices, Jira dashboards, custom fields, and plugin-dependent processes may need redesign. Self-management also means planning for administration, updates, licensing, and internal integrations. An isolated installation does not guarantee every external service will work offline.

Best for: Engineering teams whose Jira backlog is closely linked to code delivery. Test representative projects, issue relationships, and reports before moving full history.

Redmine

Redmine is an open-source project and issue tracker that teams can host on their own infrastructure. It provides an adaptable base for recording work, assigning responsibility, and following issue status.

Why it fits: It may suit teams that want to keep issue tracking under their own operational control and can keep the replacement scope focused. A straightforward defect workflow—log an issue, assign it, and update its status—provides a useful fit check.

Trade-offs: Recreating a complex Jira setup may require plugins or custom work. Those additions also become part of the isolated environment’s installation, review, and update responsibilities. Assess agile execution, reporting, and workflow details before planning migration.

Pricing: Redmine is open-source; budget for infrastructure, staff time, and any plugins or custom work.

Best for: Teams seeking self-hosted issue tracking and willing to map representative Jira projects first to identify where configuration or additional work is needed.

Taiga

Taiga focuses on Scrum and Kanban project management and has a self-hosted option. Its scope is most relevant when agile planning, rather than reproducing every part of a complex Jira setup, is the primary requirement.

Why it fits: A team can evaluate whether its backlog and board-based planning needs align with Taiga’s agile focus. This may be a reasonable direction when Jira is used mainly for Scrum or Kanban execution.

Trade-offs: Teams with extensive Jira customization, reporting, or linked development processes may need additional work to reproduce them. Do not assume automatic Jira migration: map a sample project’s issue types, states, reports, and records against the destination workflow. Installation, licensing, updates, and integrations also need an offline operating plan.

Pricing: Confirm the applicable self-hosted licensing terms for the intended team size and isolated deployment.

Best for: Teams whose central requirement is Scrum or Kanban planning and whose sample backlog and board capture the essential work.

Tuleap

Tuleap is an open-source project lifecycle management platform with agile planning and software development tools. Its self-managed positioning makes it relevant when teams want project and development workflows inside a controlled environment.

Why it fits: Teams can assess whether its project tools map to responsibilities such as backlog and release coordination. Before migration, map issue types, states, permissions, reports, and release handoffs, then identify which steps need configuration or a changed process.

Trade-offs: Complex Jira workflows should not be assumed to transfer exactly. Air-gapped operation requires a plan for updates, dependencies, backups, and integrations that might otherwise rely on external services. Evaluate the reporting and project-tracking model against actual use cases.

Pricing: Tuleap’s open-source edition is available without a license fee; commercial offerings and support may have separate terms.

Best for: Development teams seeking self-managed project lifecycle and agile tools, and prepared to map workflows and define isolated installation and maintenance procedures.

Bugzilla

Bugzilla is an open-source bug-tracking system centered on recording, assigning, and resolving defects. Teams can use it as a searchable queue with an owner and status for each reported problem.

Why it fits: It is worth considering when defect management is the main Jira workload. A team can test whether its defect fields, ownership rules, statuses, and historical records fit the Bugzilla workflow.

Trade-offs: Bugzilla is not a like-for-like Jira project-management suite. Agile boards, roadmaps, portfolio reporting, and extensive workflow customization may require other processes or tools. Air-gapped operation shifts responsibility for installation, dependencies, updates, backups, and maintenance to the organization.

Pricing: Bugzilla is open-source and has no per-seat license fee; budget for infrastructure and internal operating effort.

Best for: Teams whose priority is locally operated defect tracking, not a full recreation of Jira’s agile planning and reporting environment.

MantisBT

MantisBT is an open-source issue tracker that can be self-hosted. Its central workflow is to record an issue, assign responsibility, and follow its status.

Why it fits: It may suit teams whose main requirement is focused defect tracking inside a controlled environment. Compare a representative Jira project’s custom issue types, transitions, boards, reports, and links between work items before migration.

Trade-offs: Issue tracking alone may not cover broader project planning, agile execution, reporting, or workflow customization. Extensive Jira processes may need reconstruction and validation. Self-hosting also requires an offline plan for installation, dependencies, updates, and maintenance.

Pricing: MantisBT is open-source. Budget for hosting, maintenance, and any adaptation to local air-gap procedures; no specific paid plan or price is stated here.

Best for: Teams primarily replacing Jira’s defect intake, assignment, and status tracking. Teams that need broader planning and reporting should compare those workflows directly before selecting it.

  1. Inventory the work: List the Jira issue types, fields, users, agile routines, reports, and custom workflows that must remain usable.
  2. Separate migration from operations: Define how installation, licensing, updates, integrations, and maintenance will work inside the isolated environment.
  3. Test representative records: Compare migration steps with a sample project. For ONES.com, the documented process maps issue types, fields, and users; attachments are copied separately. See the migration guide.

Verify attachment handling separately and test your representative records and workflows before choosing it.

title: One Proxy, Three Tools, Three Different Failures: A Decision Tree for npm, Docker, and prebuild-install on Locked-Down Networks
summary:
This week I set up tooling on a corporate Windows machine behind a local proxy — 127.0.0.1:7890, the standard arrangement for developers who need to reach blocked registries. Three tools needed network access. All three failed, and each one failed differently:

  • Docker: docker pull → context deadline exceeded after 17 seconds
  • npm: worked, but 8+ seconds per registry round-trip
  • prebuild-install (the native-binary fetcher inside sqlite3): Client network socket disconnected before secure TLS connection was established

Same machine. Same network. Same proxy. The reason is the one thing most "just set your proxy" tutorials skip: every tool decides for itself whether to honor the system proxy, read environment variables, or consult its own config file. "Setting the proxy on the machine" doesn't exist. You set it per layer.

Here's the decision tree I ended up with, followed by the layers explained.

The decision tree 

A network-dependent tool fails on a proxied/censored network
│
├─ Step 0: Does the proxy itself work?
│   curl -x http://127.0.0.1:7890 -sI https://registry.npmjs.org -m 8
│   ├─ 200 → proxy is fine; your TOOL is the problem (go to Step 1)
│   └─ 000/connection refused → proxy isn't running / wrong port. Fix this first.
│
├─ Step 1: Which tool is failing? Proxy support is per-tool:
│   │
│   ├─ npm / node scripts
│   │   ├─ Reads: HTTPS_PROXY / HTTP_PROXY env vars, npm config
│   │   ├─ Slow but working? → switch registry one-off:
│   │   │     npm install  --registry=https://registry.npmmirror.com
│   │   │     (no global config change, no side effects)
│   │   └─ Totally blocked? → export HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7890
│   │
│   ├─ Docker (docker pull)
│   │   ├─ Reads: NOTHING from your shell. The daemon is a separate service.
│   │   ├─ "context deadline exceeded" = daemon can't reach the registry
│   │   └─ Fix: Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources → Proxies
│   │         set HTTP/HTTPS proxy → Apply & Restart (restart required)
│   │
│   ├─ prebuild-install / node-gyp fetchers (native binaries)
│   │   ├─ Claim to read npm_config_proxy / HTTPS_PROXY — sometimes don't
│   │   │   (my session: still died mid-TLS with proxy env set)
│   │   └─ Reliable fallback: don't fight the tool. curl the binary
│   │         from GitHub Releases yourself and drop it in place.
│   │
│   └─ curl — always explicit, always honest:
│         curl -x http://127.0.0.1:7890 -L -o file.tar.gz 
│
└─ Step 2: It "works through the proxy" but behaves weirdly?
    ├─ Shared exit IP → GitHub API 403 rate limit
    │     {"message":"API rate limit exceeded for 203.190.x.x"}
    │     Workaround: scrape the HTML asset page instead of the API:
    │     https://github.com///releases/expanded_assets/
    └─ You set a global proxy and localhost calls now break?
          → export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1  (webhooks, local servers)

Layer 0: establish ground truth with curl before touching anything

Every debugging session on a proxied network opens with the same question: is the proxy alive, and can it reach the target? Don't reason from the failing tool's output — tools muffle and relabel network errors, the same way a catch block turns "binary missing" into "package not found."

# Baseline: does the proxy work at all?
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" \
  -x http://127.0.0.1:7890 https://registry.npmjs.org -m 8
# → 200 0.4s   proxy fine, tool problem

# Compare: direct connection
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" \
  https://registry.npmjs.org -m 8
# → 200 8.0s   direct works but throttled → mirror or proxy, either is fine

The -m 8 matters more than it looks: on a broken route, a slow failure is worse than a fast one. And the gap between those two numbers tells you whether you're facing a reachability problem (use the proxy) or merely a throughput one (use a mirror).

curl earns its place here because it never lies about proxies. -x is explicit, per-command, and leaves no residue in any config file.

Layer 1: npm — the polite one

npm reads proxy configuration from multiple places and mostly behaves:

  • HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY environment variables
  • npm config (npm config set proxy http://...)

But before routing npm through a proxy, check whether you need one at all. On networks where the default registry is merely slow rather than blocked, the cleaner fix is a one-off registry flag:

npm install -g <pkg> --registry=https://registry.npmmirror.com

Notice this is deliberately not npm config set registry. A one-off flag changes nothing persistent: your other projects keep their behavior, and you never find out six months later that some internal tool was quietly hitting a mirror. Persistent config is a decision. A flag is an experiment.

Layer 2: Docker — the daemon that ignores you

This was the most instructive failure of my week:

$ docker pull n8nio/n8n
Unable to find image locally
docker: Error response from daemon: Get "https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/":
context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)

My shell had the proxy exported. curl through the proxy worked fine. So why did Docker choke?

Because docker pull isn't executed by your shell. It's a request to the Docker daemon — a separate Windows service living in its own environment. Your export HTTPS_PROXY never reaches it. The daemon tries registry-1.docker.io directly, slams into the corporate firewall, and times out with context deadline exceeded — which, notice, is itself a relabeled error: the wording suggests a timeout problem, when the actual problem is "no route."

The fix lives in the daemon's settings, not your shell:

Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources → Proxies
  Manual proxy configuration:
    Web Server (HTTP) proxy:  http://127.0.0.1:7890
    Secure Web Server (HTTPS) proxy:  http://127.0.0.1:7890
  → Apply & Restart

The restart is not optional. The daemon reads its proxy config at startup; change the settings on a running daemon and nothing changes until it comes back up.

One Windows-specific detail worth knowing: 127.0.0.1 in Docker Desktop's proxy settings correctly refers to the host machine. This is one of the few places where localhost-in-a-config "just works" for Docker on Windows.

Layer 3: prebuild-install — when the tool's proxy support betrays you

Native modules (sqlite3, bcrypt, canvas, sharp) download prebuilt binaries from GitHub Releases during npm install. When that download fails, npm install still exits 0. The failure detonates later, at runtime — I wrote a whole separate post about that trap.

The fetcher (prebuild-install) documents proxy support via npm_config_proxy / npm_config_https_proxy. In my session, with both set, it still died:

prebuild-install warn install Client network socket disconnected
before secure TLS connection was established

That message usually means the connection was reset mid-handshake — the signature of a direct connection to a blocked host, i.e. the proxy config never took effect for that request. Whether that's a bug in the version I had, or some subtlety about which env var it reads in which mode, I honestly can't say.

What I can say: the reliable move is to stop negotiating with the tool.

# 1. Find the real asset name (N-API naming, NOT node-vXXX — see below)
curl -sSL "https://github.com/TryGhost/node-sqlite3/releases/expanded_assets/v5.1.7" \
  | grep -o 'href="[^"]*"' | grep -i "win32-x64"

# 2. Fetch it with curl, which you've already proven works
curl -sSL -x http://127.0.0.1:7890 -o binding.tar.gz \
  "https://github.com/TryGhost/node-sqlite3/releases/download/v5.1.7/sqlite3-v5.1.7-napi-v6-win32-x64.tar.gz"

# 3. Place it: the tarball contains build/Release/node_sqlite3.node,
#    so extract at the PACKAGE ROOT — not into build/Release
tar -xzf binding.tar.gz -C .../node_modules/sqlite3

This week I set up tooling on a corporate Windows machine behind a local proxy — 127.0.0.1:7890, the standard arrangement for developers who need to reach blocked registries. Three tools needed network access. All three failed, and each one failed differently:

│

│   │   │     (no global config change, no side effects)

│
└─ Step 2: It "works through the proxy" but behaves weirdly?
    ├─ Shared exit IP → GitHub API 403 rate limit

    └─ You set a global proxy and localhost calls now break?

Layer 0: establish ground truth with curl before touching anything

Every debugging session on a proxied network opens with the same question: is the proxy alive, and can it reach the target? Don't reason from the failing tool's output — tools muffle and relabel network errors, the same way a catch block turns "binary missing" into "package not found."

# Baseline: does the proxy work at all?
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" \
  -x http://127.0.0.1:7890 https://registry.npmjs.org -m 8
# → 200 0.4s   proxy fine, tool problem

# Compare: direct connection
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" \
  https://registry.npmjs.org -m 8
# → 200 8.0s   direct works but throttled → mirror or proxy, either is fine

The -m 8 matters more than it looks: on a broken route, a slow failure is worse than a fast one. And the gap between those two numbers tells you whether you're facing a reachability problem (use the proxy) or merely a throughput one (use a mirror).

curl earns its place here because it never lies about proxies. -x is explicit, per-command, and leaves no residue in any config file.

title: HyperPod Slurm Clusters Declare Node Software Through Managed Extensions
summary:
TL;DR

  • A cluster extension is a software package that AWS manages on every node of a SageMaker HyperPod Slurm cluster, declared through an API or the console and then installed, updated and removed by the service on the whole fleet.
  • Amazon launched the feature in November 2026 with two extensions: sagemaker-observability, which ships node, GPU, EFA and Slurm metrics to CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and sagemaker-user-management, which creates the same user and group IDs on every node and rules who may use SSH and sudo.
  • The extension service runs its software as root on every node, so CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension and DeleteClusterExtension belong with administrator permissions, and the post advises keeping them away from the cluster execution role because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use that role's credentials.
  • Status carries the operational weight: Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when no node reports a problem, with ActiveCount and TotalCount showing whether every node has converged, and Degraded when some nodes failed.
  • Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own user management while a monitoring team owns observability, and the post asks for one owner per component so a script and an extension never configure the same exporter.
  • Lifecycle scripts stay the right tool for organization-specific software such as security agents, license servers and storage layout, and the two approaches coexist as long as each component keeps a single owner.
  • Slurm's maintenance reservations provide a separately planned mechanism for fleet-level work: root or SlurmUser creates the reservation, the maintenance flag marks its purpose, and a reservation with nodes stays inside one partition.

Official AWS figure from the 20 November 2026 post: the declaration path from administrator to cluster, the validation step, and convergence of the extension onto every node group, including replacement nodes. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

Amazon Web Services published Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on 20 November 2026, and the launch starts with two extensions. Two extensions exist today. What matters is that the software on the nodes now has a declared, validated, reportable form, which is the layer that used to live in a script somebody edited on a Friday.

What a cluster extension owns on a HyperPod Slurm fleet

HyperPod already declares most of a cluster through an API: node roles and partitions, FSx for Lustre and OpenZFS mounts, minimum capacity, automatic topology management and deep health checks that stress GPUs and test NCCL connectivity. The post describes those as five layers that HyperPod applies once, when it provisions a node, and then names the sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, as the one that keeps changing for the life of the cluster.

Netics editorial visual, 21 November 2026: the two mechanisms side by side, with the behaviour that changes when a node is replaced.

The reason is mundane and familiar to anyone who has run a shared compute estate. Researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, an exporter ships a fix. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet, and a mistake appears only when it executes on some node. The extension replaces that cycle with a declaration, a schema check and a status field.

Two extensions ship today: metrics, and identity across nodes

The observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter and Slurm job and cluster metrics, and sends them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. The user management extension creates users and groups with the same IDs on every node, controls who can use SSH and sudo per node type, registers users with Slurm accounting, and can connect the cluster to Active Directory through a directory service.

Official AWS console capture from the 20 November 2026 post: installing sagemaker-observability, with the metric level and collection interval as the settings a schema validates before anything reaches a node. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

Those two choices say something about where AWS sees the pain. FSx mounts, network topology and scheduler configuration already had declarative paths. Identity and telemetry are the parts that drift silently, because a mismatched UID shows up as an unreadable home directory months later and a missing exporter shows up as a gap in a dashboard nobody was watching. The post also notes that each extension has its own ARN, which turns one cluster into several ownership zones.

The service runs as root, so the API belongs to administrators

The post states the permission model in one sentence worth repeating to a security team: an extension runs software as root on every node. That makes the three management calls administrative operations, and the recommendation that follows is specific and easy to get wrong: keep CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension and DeleteClusterExtension away from the cluster's execution role, because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use that role's credentials.

Official AWS console capture from the 20 November 2026 post: both extensions in one view, each with its version, status and configuration link. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

The execution role still needs a narrow set of permissions, and the list is a good map of what each extension touches. Observability needs CloudWatch or aps:RemoteWrite. User management needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the Active Directory secrets, kms:Decrypt when those secrets use a customer managed key, and a shared file system for home directories. A team that grants all of it through one broad role gets the fleet-wide root access the post warns about, with the convenience of a single policy.

Schema validation deserves an honest reading here. HyperPod checks settings against the extension's schema and rejects a misspelled setting before anything reaches a node, which removes a whole class of failed rollouts. It cannot know whether a metric interval matches the cardinality your Prometheus can absorb, or whether the user list matches the directory your staff actually use. Those remain engineering decisions with an owner.

Official AWS figure from the 20 November 2026 post: the status progression from Creating through Active and Updating to Degraded, with a health issue that names the component, its effect on the cluster, the next step and the number of affected nodes. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

Active status plus the node summary show whether every node reports the requested version

Status is where this design earns its keep. Creating or Updating marks a rollout in progress. Active status plus the node summary show whether every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem. Degraded means some nodes failed or report an issue. Each health issue names the component, describes the effect on the cluster, gives the next step and counts the affected nodes.

Provisioning scripts provide no built-in inventory of what is installed. A team running an exporter through a provisioning script learns about drift from a dashboard gap, or from a researcher who notices a missing GPU counter. ActiveCount and TotalCount provide the fleet-wide check beyond the node you happened to log into, and they show when a fleet-wide change has converged.

Netics editorial visual, 21 November 2026: the layers HyperPod derives at provision time, and the software layer added in November 2026.

The console view also shows the ownership split working. A cluster running both extensions lists them separately, with versions, statuses and configuration links, which is what allows one team to own metrics and another to own identity without sharing an API call.

The continuing role of lifecycle scripts

The post is clear about the boundary: run extensions when HyperPod offers a managed capability, and keep custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software and initialization. Security agents, license servers and the storage layout a data pipeline expects belong in the image, because only your team knows what they need.

The rule that makes coexistence work is ownership. A component should have one owner, and the post warns against managing the same exporter, user or service through both a script and an extension, since competing configurations cause installation and runtime conflicts. Migration advice follows the same logic: turn the capability off in the lifecycle scripts, upload them to S3 so new nodes skip it, and move one capability at a time.

The SageMaker AI developer guide page on cluster extensions, with the requirements, the two available extensions and their scope. Source: docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm-extensions.html, captured 21 November 2026.

What Slurm's maintenance reservations explain about the timing

A fleet-wide software change on a shared cluster needs a window, and Slurm already has the mechanism for it. The scheduler's advanced reservation guide describes reservations created, updated and destroyed by root or the configured SlurmUser through scontrol, a maintenance reservation created with the maint flag, and the rule that a reservation containing nodes stays inside a single partition; the guide's own example reserves the whole machine at 16:00 for 120 minutes with the maint and ignore_jobs flags.

The scheduling consequence is practical. HyperPod uses Slurm maintenance reservations to keep jobs off nodes during deep health checks; the extension guide says extension rollout itself does not hold back job scheduling. A team that pairs the extension update with a reservation it controls gets a predictable drain, and one that skips the reservation finds out how a degraded extension behaves while jobs are running.

Netics editorial visual, 21 November 2026: the part of the configuration a schema settles, and the part that needs a decision from the team that runs the cluster.

The launch is worth adopting for the two components it covers today, and the design is worth copying for the question it asks about every other component on the nodes: who owns it, how often does it change, and does a status field exist that says whether the whole fleet agrees. Teams running their own GPU estate outside a managed cluster face the same question with fewer defaults, which is the territory the self-hosted infrastructure and cloud exit page explores. For a separate SageMaker topic, see SageMaker's cross-region inference router.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

Each health issue names the component, describes the effect on the cluster, gives the next step and counts the affected nodes.

Provisioning scripts provide no built-in inventory of what is installed. A team running an exporter through a provisioning script learns about drift from a dashboard gap, or from a researcher who notices a missing GPU counter. ActiveCount and TotalCount provide the fleet-wide check beyond the node you happened to log into, and they show when a fleet-wide change has converged.

The console view also shows the ownership split working. A cluster running both extensions lists them separately, with versions, statuses and configuration links, which is what allows one team to own metrics and another to own identity without sharing an API call.

The continuing role of lifecycle scripts

The post is clear about the boundary: run extensions when HyperPod offers a managed capability, and keep custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software and initialization. Security agents, license servers and the storage layout a data pipeline expects belong in the image, because only your team knows what they need.

The rule that makes coexistence work is ownership. A component should have one owner, and the post warns against managing the same exporter, user or service through both a script and an extension, since competing configurations cause installation and runtime conflicts. Migration advice follows the same logic: turn the capability off in the lifecycle scripts, upload them to S3 so new nodes skip it, and move one capability at a time.

What Slurm's maintenance reservations explain about the timing

A fleet-wide software change on a shared cluster needs a window, and Slurm already has the mechanism for it. The scheduler's advanced reservation guide describes reservations created, updated and destroyed by root or the configured SlurmUser through scontrol, a maintenance reservation created with the maint flag, and the rule that a reservation containing nodes stays inside a single partition; the guide's own example reserves the whole machine at 16:00 for 120 minutes with the maint and ignore_jobs flags.

The scheduling consequence is practical. HyperPod uses Slurm maintenance reservations to keep jobs off nodes during deep health checks; the extension guide says extension rollout itself does not hold back job scheduling. A team that pairs the extension update with a reservation it controls gets a predictable drain, and one that skips the reservation finds out how a degraded extension behaves while jobs are running.
